blogs.title: Filtering and reducing AI agent telemetry with the OpenTelemetry Collector
blogs.content: Posted on October 22, 2026 by Adnan Rahic, Bindplane by Dynatrace CNCF projects highlighted in this post Turn on an AI coding agent’s telemetry and it throws a wall of text at you. It’s expensive to store and what’s worse, you can’t make sense of it. It’s all OpenTelemetry native, though. So you can shape it in the Collector before sending it to a telemetry backend. Which leaves one question. What do you actually need? The requirement isn’t to collect less, it’s to keep what answers questions I gave Claude Code a small task. Fix two failing tests, add a few boundary tests. It did. With every content flag on, that one run produced 181 telemetry records and 289 KB of JSON. What I needed was answers to these six questions: Question What answers it What is this costing, per model? claude_code.cost.usage Tokens per session, and how much is cache? claude_code.token.usage by type Which tools fail, and how often? tool_result events, success Are people rejecting the agent’s edits? tool_decision events Where is the latency? llm_request spans, ttft_ms What broke? api_error events, error_class Every answer is a counter or a short attribute. I don’t need prompts, file bodies or diffs. If no dashboard, alert, or query reads a field, it isn’t observability. It’s storage you’re paying to index. Where the volume actually lives An agent runs a loop: Prompt, model call, tool call, result, decide, repeat. One interaction is a claude_code.interaction span with an llm_request child per model turn and a tool child per tool call. With OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT on, each tool span gets a tool.output event holding whatever the tool returned. That’s a directory listing. When the tool is Read, the event is the file. A 40 KB file becomes a 40 KB span event. Logs have the same shape. tool_result and tool_decision events carry tool_parameters, the full arguments to the tool. For a Write that’s the whole file. Same content as the span event, stored twice. Metrics carry identity instead. Every data point has session.id, user.id, user.email and two account ids. Each new session created a fresh set of time series that never goes away. Twenty five sessions gave me 300 series for eight metrics. The default instrumentation is written for debugging one agent run, not for running a fleet. Tool content lands in traces and logs both. Metrics are keyed on attributes that belong on the resource, or nowhere. None of that is wrong for a single developer watching a single session. It’s wrong at 200 sessions a day. The agent won’t change its defaults for you, so the pipeline has to. What we’re building One OTLP receiver that’ll ingest Claude Code’s internal telemetry. Every signal is fanned into two pipelines, a raw one and an optimized one, each with its own exporter, all six landing in the same Grafana LGTM container. The raw pipeline is the control group. It carries a service.name and a batch processor. Nothing else. The optimized pipeline carries the processors we’ll add in this tutorial. The same receiver feeds both, so both paths see byte identical input. That’s what makes the comparison honest. Both data sets land in Grafana. One dashboard reads both and draws them side by side, red for raw, green for optimized. Cardinality, bytes per minute, record counts. The gap between the lines is the storage you stop paying for. In production you’d point the raw exporters at object storage, or drop them altogether. Here they point at Grafana because I want to show you the difference. # docker-compose.yaml services: lgtm: image: grafana/otel-lgtm:0.33.1 ports: - "3000:3000" collector: image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.161.0 depends_on: [lgtm] volumes: - ./config.yaml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml:ro ports: - "4317:4317" - "4318:4318" receivers: otlp: protocols: grpc: endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317 http: endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318 exporters: otlp/lgtm_raw_logs: endpoint: lgtm:4317 tls: insecure: true sending_queue: enabled: true otlp/lgtm_opt_logs: endpoint: lgtm:4317 tls: insecure: true sending_queue: enabled: true # four more exactly like this: # otlp/lgtm_raw_metrics, otlp/lgtm_raw_traces, # otlp/lgtm_opt_metrics, otlp/lgtm_opt_traces service: pipelines: logs/raw: receivers: [otlp] processors: [batch] exporters: [otlp/lgtm_raw_logs] logs/optimized: receivers: [otlp] processors: [batch] # the reduction goes here exporters: [otlp/lgtm_opt_logs] # four more exactly like this: # metrics/raw, metrics/optimized, traces/raw, traces/optimized export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 export CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1 export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp export OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317 export OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 export OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1 export OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 export OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 Step 2. Logs: Drop, delete, trim, hash Filter. api_request carries a model name and a request id. Everything else on it lives in other signals. Drop the whole event. Roughly a quarter of log records. processors: filter/drop_api_request: error_mode: ignore logs: log_record: - 'attributes["event.name"] == "api_request"' Delete. Six attributes off every record. tool_parameters is the big one. prompt_length and response_length stay, so you still see size trends without the text. transform/logs_delete_fields: error_mode: ignore log_statements: - context: log statements: - delete_key(log.attributes, "prompt") - delete_key(log.attributes, "response") - delete_key(log.attributes, "tool_parameters") - delete_key(log.attributes, "workspace.host_paths") - delete_key(log.attributes, "user.email") - delete_key(log.attributes, "terminal.type") Hash and trim. Hash session.id and user.id, cap error at 256 characters. transform/logs_hash_and_trim: error_mode: ignore log_statements: - context: log statements: - set(log.attributes["session.id"], Substring(SHA256(log.attributes["session.id"]), 0, 16)) where log.attributes["session.id"] != nil - set(log.attributes["user.id"], Substring(SHA256(log.attributes["user.id"]), 0, 16)) where log.attributes["user.id"] != nil - set(log.attributes["error"], Substring(log.attributes["error"], 0, 256)) where log.attributes["error"] != nil and Len(log.attributes["error"]) > 256 Truncate the digest. A full SHA256 is 64 characters replacing a 36 character UUID, twice per record. The first time I ran this, log bytes went up. Sixteen hex characters is plenty. logs/optimized: receivers: [otlp] processors: [filter/drop_api_request, transform/logs_delete_fields, transform/logs_hash_and_trim, batch] exporters: [otlp/lgtm_opt_logs] Log bytes roughly halve. Step 3. Metrics: Delete the dimension The problem here is cardinality, not bytes. Delete six attributes from every data point and 300 series become 12 regardless if the content flags are on or off. transform/metrics_delete_fields: error_mode: ignore metric_statements: - context: datapoint statements: - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "session.id") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.account_uuid") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.account_id") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.id") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "user.email") - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "terminal.type") Sum the sessions, then convert. Claude Code exports delta temporality and Prometheus wants cumulative, so delta_to_cumulative has to sit at the end of this pipeline. With session.id gone, every running session writes into the same twelve series, and the converter only accepts points in timestamp order. Sum the sessions per window first. # 1. Collect two seconds of exports. The size is out of reach on purpose, # so the timeout is always what flushes. batch/metrics_window: send_batch_size: 1000000 send_batch_max_size: 0 timeout: 2s # 2. Put every metric of the same name under one resource. gr...
